quests.hint: Buying tickets today for a concert that happens next month.
quests.explanation: PRE- means 'before the event.' PRE- + BOOK = PREBOOK, to reserve something ahead of time. RE- would instead mean booking a second time, which fits a very different situation, like fixing a cancelled reservation.
quests.instruction: RE- means 'again.' PRE- means 'before.' Which one fits here?

quests.hint: Calling the airline a second time because your first call got disconnected.
quests.explanation: RE- ('again') fits RECALL in this sense, repeating an action already attempted. PRE- would instead mean calling before something happens, which doesn't match a follow-up call after a dropped line.
quests.instruction: RE- means 'again.' PRE- means 'before.' Which one fits here?

quests.hint: A word that means 'to guess an outcome before it happens,' based on evidence you already have.
quests.explanation: PREDICT is PRE- ('before') + DICT ('say'), to say what will happen before it does. Notice it isn't REDICT — there's no 'saying again' involved, only anticipating the future.
quests.instruction: RE- means 'again.' PRE- means 'before.' Which one fits here?

quests.hint: Taking off a jacket you had zipped up a moment earlier.
quests.explanation: UN- reverses a specific, often physical action — ZIP becomes UNZIP, the exact opposite motion. DIS- tends to attach to more abstract ideas (agreement, comfort) rather than a simple physical reversal like this.
quests.instruction: UN- reverses an action. DIS- often means 'not' for more abstract ideas. Which fits here?

quests.hint: Two business partners ending their working relationship after years together.
quests.explanation: DISSOLVE (as in DISSOLVE a partnership) uses DIS- because it's describing an abstract relationship ending, not a physical object being reversed. UN- typically doesn't attach this way — 'unsolve' means something else entirely (to work out an unsolved case).
quests.instruction: UN- reverses an action. DIS- often means 'not' for more abstract ideas. Which fits here?

quests.hint: Removing the plug from the wall so an appliance is no longer connected to power.
quests.explanation: UN- + PLUG = UNPLUG, the direct physical reversal of plugging something in. DIS- would sound unnatural here — English speakers don't say 'displug,' since UN- is the prefix this specific action takes.
quests.instruction: UN- reverses an action. DIS- often means 'not' for more abstract ideas. Which fits here?

quests.hint: Sending a package to the wrong address by accident because you swapped two digits.
quests.explanation: MIS- + DIRECT = MISDIRECT, to send or guide something incorrectly, by mistake. DIS- would instead suggest actively refusing to direct something, not simply making an error.
quests.instruction: MIS- means 'wrongly.' DIS- means 'not/the opposite of.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: A teenager who ignores their curfew and stays out anyway, on purpose.
quests.explanation: DIS- + OBEY = DISOBEY, to deliberately not follow a rule. This is a choice, not an accident — which is exactly why it takes DIS- ('not') instead of MIS- ('wrongly, by mistake').
quests.instruction: MIS- means 'wrongly.' DIS- means 'not/the opposite of.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: Repeating a rumor because you got a key fact confused with someone else's story.
quests.explanation: MIS- + INFORM = MISINFORM, to give someone incorrect information, typically without meaning to. The error is the key idea — that's the signal for MIS-, not DIS-.
quests.instruction: MIS- means 'wrongly.' DIS- means 'not/the opposite of.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: A student who takes on five extra classes and ends up exhausted every night.
quests.explanation: OVER- + LOAD = OVERLOAD, to load with too much, beyond a reasonable limit. UNDER- would describe the opposite problem: too little of something.
quests.instruction: OVER- means 'too much.' UNDER- means 'too little.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: A road with far fewer streetlights than a busy area actually needs at night.
quests.explanation: UNDER- + LIT = UNDERLIT, lit less than is needed or expected. OVER- would instead describe a space that's far too bright, the opposite issue.
quests.instruction: OVER- means 'too much.' UNDER- means 'too little.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: A patient given far more medicine than the correct dose calls for.
quests.explanation: OVER- + MEDICATE = OVERMEDICATE, to give too much medicine. UNDER- would instead mean giving too little — both are real medical concerns, but they describe opposite mistakes.
quests.instruction: OVER- means 'too much.' UNDER- means 'too little.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: A tank completely filled to the brim with fresh water.
quests.explanation: -FUL means 'full of.' TANK... isn't the pattern here — think instead of a simpler word: CUP + -FUL = CUPFUL, containing as much as a cup can hold. -LESS would mean the opposite: containing none at all.
quests.instruction: -FUL means 'full of.' -LESS means 'without.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: A night sky in the countryside with absolutely no clouds blocking the stars.
quests.explanation: -LESS forms CLOUDLESS from CLOUD, without any clouds. -FUL would instead describe a sky packed with clouds — the exact opposite weather.
quests.instruction: -FUL means 'full of.' -LESS means 'without.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: A meeting packed with useful takeaways that everyone can apply right away.
quests.explanation: -FUL builds USEFUL from USE, full of use or value. Compare USELESS from earlier: same root, opposite suffix, opposite meaning — a clean example of how one suffix swap flips a word's sense entirely.
quests.instruction: -FUL means 'full of.' -LESS means 'without.' Which fits here?

quests.hint: The special quality that makes a rare gem worth so much money.
quests.explanation: -ITY names an abstract, often more technical or formal quality: RARE + -ITY = RARITY, the state of being uncommon. -NESS tends to attach to everyday, plain-spoken adjectives instead (like KINDNESS or SADNESS).
quests.meaningBreakdown: RAR (root) + ITY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: -NESS and -ITY both form nouns of quality, but pair with different roots. Which fits here?

quests.hint: The comfortable, plain feeling of an old pair of jeans you've worn for years.
quests.explanation: -NESS forms SOFTNESS from SOFT, a simple everyday quality. -ITY doesn't attach to SOFT in standard English — 'softity' isn't a word, showing these two suffixes aren't interchangeable despite similar jobs.
quests.meaningBreakdown: SOFT (root) + NESS (suffix, forms a noun of state)
quests.instruction: -NESS and -ITY both form nouns of quality, but pair with different roots. Which fits here?

quests.hint: The trait that lets a gymnast bend and twist her body into difficult positions.
quests.explanation: FLEXIBILITY combines FLEXIBLE (itself FLEX + -IBLE) with -ITY, naming the quality of being flexible. This is a more technical, physical-science-flavored word — exactly the register where -ITY tends to appear over -NESS.
quests.meaningBreakdown: FLEXIBIL (root) + ITY (suffix, forms a noun of quality)
quests.instruction: -NESS and -ITY both form nouns of quality, but pair with different roots. Which fits here?

quests.hint: Someone who builds houses and other structures for a living.
quests.explanation: -ER often attaches to plain, everyday action verbs: BUILD + -ER = BUILDER, a person who builds. -IST tends to appear with fields of study or belief instead, like SCIENTIST or ARTIST.
quests.instruction: -ER and -IST both name a person, but attach to different kinds of roots. Which fits here?

quests.hint: Someone whose profession is analyzing numbers and predicting the economy.
quests.explanation: ECONOMIST is ECONOMY + -IST (the Y drops), a person specializing in a field of study. -ER doesn't attach here — 'economer' isn't standard English, since fields of expertise typically pair with -IST.
quests.instruction: Which word matches this situation?

quests.hint: Someone hired to fix leaky pipes and install new bathroom fixtures.
quests.explanation: -ER forms PLUMBER from PLUMB, a person who does a specific everyday trade. -IST would sound out of place here — trades and hands-on jobs generally pick -ER over -IST.
quests.instruction: -ER and -IST both name a person, but attach to different kinds of roots. Which fits here?

quests.hint: The formal act of officially starting a new law or government program.
quests.explanation: IMPLEMENTATION combines IMPLEMENT with -TION, naming the process of carrying a plan into effect. Notice IMPLEMENT itself already ends in -MENT (as a base word), while the action of doing it takes -TION on top.
quests.meaningBreakdown: IMPLEMENT (root) + TION (suffix, forms a noun of process)
quests.instruction: -MENT and -TION both form nouns from verbs, but each verb picks only one. Which fits here?

quests.hint: The excitement felt right before a long-awaited trip finally begins.
quests.explanation: -MENT forms EXCITEMENT from EXCITE, the state of being excited. -TION doesn't attach to EXCITE in standard English — 'excitation' exists but means something more technical (like exciting a particle in physics), not everyday enthusiasm.
quests.meaningBreakdown: EXCITE (root) + MENT (suffix, forms a noun of state)
quests.instruction: -MENT and -TION both form nouns from verbs, but each verb picks only one. Which fits here?

quests.hint: The formal process a company follows to hire and bring on new staff.
quests.explanation: RECRUITMENT is RECRUIT + -MENT, the process or act of recruiting. Like EXCITEMENT, this verb has settled on -MENT rather than -TION — there's no consistent rule, so recognizing common pairings by ear matters.
quests.meaningBreakdown: RECRUIT (root) + MENT (suffix, forms a noun of process)
quests.instruction: -MENT and -TION both form nouns from verbs, but each verb picks only one. Which fits here?

quests.hint: A signature on a contract that can be checked against a known sample to confirm it's genuine.
quests.explanation: -IBLE, a close cousin of -ABLE, also means 'capable of being.' VERIFY + -IBLE = VERIFIABLE (with a spelling shift), capable of being verified. Both suffixes carry the same meaning; the specific root determines which spelling English settled on.
quests.instruction: -ABLE and -IBLE mean the same thing, but each root has one correct spelling. Which fits here?

quests.hint: A rule so clearly written that everyone in the room interprets it the same way.
quests.explanation: UNDERSTANDABLE takes -ABLE, not -IBLE — English roots ending in a full, standalone word (like UNDERSTAND) almost always pair with -ABLE, while -IBLE tends to appear on roots that aren't complete words by themselves (like VERIF- or POSS-).
quests.instruction: -ABLE and -IBLE mean the same thing, but each root has one correct spelling. Which fits here?

quests.hint: A single seat left on a fully booked flight, ready to be reserved by the next customer.
quests.explanation: -IBLE completes POSSIBLE from POSS- (an incomplete root borrowed from Latin, meaning 'able'). Since POSS- isn't a standalone English word, it takes -IBLE rather than -ABLE — a useful pattern for guessing which spelling a new word needs.
quests.instruction: -ABLE and -IBLE mean the same thing, but each root has one correct spelling. Which fits here?

quests.hint: Review: a word describing something you can't see through, versus something you can predict is coming.
quests.explanation: This unit trained you to tell related affixes apart: RE- ('again') from PRE- ('before'), UN- (physical reversal) from DIS- (abstract negation), and MIS- (an honest error) from DIS- (a deliberate refusal). VISIBLE takes -IBLE because VIS- isn't a standalone word, following the same pattern as POSSIBLE.
quests.instruction: Review: which suffix fits a root that isn't a complete word on its own?

quests.hint: Review: someone whose entire career is devoted to studying and teaching economics at a university.
quests.explanation: -IST names a person tied to a field or belief, distinct from -ER, which usually names a person doing an everyday action. ECONOMIST fits the field-and-expertise pattern you practiced earlier in this unit.
quests.instruction: Review: which suffix names a person devoted to a field of study?

quests.hint: Review: a container completely full of coins, versus a wallet with nothing in it at all.
quests.explanation: -FUL ('full of') and -LESS ('without') are true opposites, unlike -NESS and -ITY, which mean nearly the same thing but pair with different roots. JARFUL fits the first pattern: full to the amount a jar can hold.
quests.instruction: Review: which suffix means 'full of,' the opposite of -LESS?
